tweets.text: Longer thread on why 'legitimate' crypto use cases never take off. Lets imagine a real use case of crypto built around social participation in a common enterprise. For this example, lets assume a communal dog-walking platform is a legitimately wholesome and workable enterprise. Adam creates DogeWalk, a fun application for dogowners and dog lovers around the world to connect and dog lovers can sign up to walk the dogs of the dogowners. In order to maintain trust but anonymity amongst the participants, Adam decides to incorporate crypto into DogeWalk, allowing crypto payments and Walk points, a reputation system which supports the legitimacy of the participant. DogeWalk takes off amongst a community of dogwalkers. Turns out that there is legitimate demand for people to walk dogs in an anonymous manner. Adam makes some money from platform fees charged on his some 1,000 users. Bob sees DogeWalk taking off and sees an opportunity. He creates PupStroll as a competitor to DogeWalk and informs the PupStroll users that they can get a piece of PupStroll! Instead of giving all the fees to Adam, together they can share in the decentralized ownership of a dog walking platform! PupStroll is almost exactly like DogeWalk, except PupStroll users get Stroll points, and a referral link. DogeWalk users start moving to PupStroll. PupStroll does a token launch and suddenly everyone is talking about how the future of dog walking is decentralized. People who have never walked a dog in their lives start signing up with PupStroll to walk dogs and farm season 2 of the STROLL airdrop. Charlie sees PupStroll take off and trade at an implied FDV of 20m with 5,000 users. He raises $500,000 from a venture capital fund BrandName Capital by selling 10% of the future supply of HoundTrek. HoundTrek is almost exactly like PupStroll except it has a slightly cooler 'dark mode' UI. Charlie proudly announces his funding round and launches an aggressive points and referral programme. He even provides zero fees and bonus payments, funded from BrandName Capital's investment. PupStroll's users start moving over to HoundTrek given the economic incentives. The price of STROLL declines and angry purchasers of STROLL begin yelling at Bob for not keeping up with HoundTrek. Bob simply does not have the firepower to match. PupStroll's users give up on season 2. HoundTrek announces a second funding round right before TGE, led by DarkArts Capital. DarkArts Capital purchases another 10% of TREK allegedly at a valuation of $20,000,000 but really at a valuation of $10,000,000. HoundTrek launches the TREK token which opens at 25m FDV alongside a small airdrop. The TREK token climbs steadily upward for a while as Charlie uses the funds raised to provide price support while paying for marketing. When the token reaches 100m FDV, DarkArts Capital and BrandName Capital take profit on the token. Number goes down. Everyone gets mad at BrandName Capital and DarkArts Capital. David who sees all these play out, realizes that there is an opportunity. "Tis all the fault of the greedy venture capital funds!" he says. We need "true community ownership!" With that, he opens a funding round for WanderPooch via an 'ICO', valuing WanderPooch at 'only 10m'. He raises 2m of capital. David knows nothing about dogs nor dogwalking platforms. He simply pays himself the money and shuts down the project after a year. Eugene is a former venture capital hotshot. He pulls together a coalition of his VC friends and raises 10m at a 100m valuation to break the dogwalking industry once and for all. CanineHike is the cleanest dogwalking application ever, and in order to generate demand on both sides, he even invests the money into cute dogs for dogwalkers to walk! He pays ever KOL that was early to PupStroll, promising them both money and tokens for writing long threads on why decentralized dogwalking will work this time. To increase platform metrics, Eugene even pays an agency which hires homeless people to walk dogs on CanineHike! Eugene doesn't even like dogs but the marketing works. On TGE, the token trades at 1bn FDV through clever supply control, marketing and a limited airdrop. Eugene dangles a season 2, while amplifying those who made life changing money farming the airdrop. Meanwhile him and his VC friends sell locked tokens at a 60% discount on secondaries. Within 6 months, the HIKE token declines in price. And at the end of it all, decentralised dog walking is decried as a scam by retail users who do not like dogs as they scream at builders who do not like dogs who have been funded by investors who do not like dogs. As for Adam and the people that actually wanted to walk dogs? Yeah they just do it between themselves in hobbyist groups now and will never touch crypto again.

tweets.text: RT @0xKolten: Here’s my longer thoughts on why this is bad. First off, wtf? We’re in the middle of a DeFi and TradFi convergence that builders have been scratching and clawing towards for a decade, primarily centered around yield, and we’re proposing nuking the underlying engine? The staking yield is the base rate of DeFi and everything prices off it. Lending rates, vault strategies, the cost of borrowing stablecoins against ETH collateral, all of it references the staking rate as the floor. This proposal tapers that floor to zero, and when the yield on staked ETH drops below the cost to borrow it, the looping strategies that generate the majority of ETH borrow demand invert. Borrowers will unwind, borrow demand will collapse, LSTs lose the yield that made them worth holding over plain ETH, stablecoin borrowers who were quietly offsetting interest costs with staking yield face a higher real cost, utilization drops, and suppliers earn less. tweets.text: RT @IsdrsP: I think that EIP 8361 tries to do too many things (increasing the moneyness of ETH, pre-empting remotely possible future decreases security due to overstake, protecting solo stakers, etc) at once and in my estimation will mostly do the opposite. I honestly believe that issuance change is too complicated to treat with this urgency, that the far-future concerns are drastically overblown, and it's very bad timing to introduce such a divisive proposal, especially in such a way. It has also been pushed last minute in an attempt to squeeze into Hegota (still subject to the EIP Inclusion process), even though potential issuance changes had been communicated as per the current strawmap to be slated for I* at the earliest. IMO, this proposal lays Ethereum's hard-fought uniqueness (real decentralization and neutrality) at the sacrificial altar of ETH as money, camouflaged against an insufficiently scrutinized concept of "minimally viable" security spend. Unfortunately, it also doesn't come to terms with the fact the moral hazard of a "too big to fail" event is not necessarily mitigated by limiting staking adoption, only displaced, as ETH seeking yield will mostly just go to more risky and likely custodial solutions, in my estimation thereby increasing the likelihood of such an event. Apart from misgivings around the governance and consensus (or lack thereof, given its wide-reaching scope and implications) process around this proposal, I find that the selective supporting research is too theoretical and is lacking from a macro, micro and behavioral economic modeling perspective, especially with regards to 2nd and 3rd order effects. This applies to especially to two aspects: 1) one of the central theses around the urgent concern about the stake rate (which is lower than most other PoS networks which are mostly fine) that also hinges on the idea that just because issuance is positive at 100% stake then there's necessarily incentive to do so (ignoring years of economic history and literature which illustrate that demand is actually expressed as a complex function of utility, and not merely purely theoretic expected value, and strong contra examples such as USD as cash/savings vs T-Bills); and 2) on the effect of drastically reduced issuance (and real validator rewards) on the resulting validator set, and the negative externalities that will be born out of this material change in monetary policy (and possible further changes which might be required for correction). Due to the new proposed curve a very real possibility of a sustained equilibrium at or near 50% of Ethereum staked with 0 nominal (nevermind real) yield is now possible, which would essentially be a death-knell for the security of the network, as node operators and staking protocols which prioritize expertise, decentralization, and expensive know-how are priced out and large, centralized, minimal-cost parties take over the operation of the overwhelming majority of the network's validators. Unfortunately, at current ETH/USD prices, such a scenario isn't even necessary for this proposed issuance change to lead to a large consolidation of the operator set, which would drastically lower the network's Nakamoto coefficient and thus its resilience. In an eventuality where few actors are allowed to control one of the fundamental levers of the network -- determining its security (i.e. control of fork choice) -- by simply being able to offer staking at break-even or at a loss for long enough to price most other actors out of the market, what will be left of Ethereum's neutrality when the only recourse (now made ever-more necessary) will be a substantial and messy social slashing? I'm not against an issuance reduction in general; I am against an issuance reduction without centering on the core questions, and giving the community adequate time, tools, and analysis to be able to consider the bevy of implications. To me these core questions are: * What is the right amount of economic security given that we want Ethereum to be the centerpiece of onchain finance? A minimum viable security approach here doesn't cut it -- nation states don't think this way and the largest financial network in the world shouldn't either * What is the effect of the market structures generated by any issuance curve, the relevant expected prices of operation (eg in ETH/fiat terms), and the effect of issuance changes -- and their consequences -- on demand for the asset, especially on the underlying validator and node operator set? * How does the network retain its neutrality, utility, and demand, if social slashing is utilized not in the same way that nuclear arms are (as a last-measure deterrent) but rather as as the go-to solution for problems created by the network's own security paradigm? * Why do we honestly believe that the terminal staking rate is in the high double digits? What practical economic modelling or historical indicators are there to point towards this? * Are we okay with a hyper-centralized validator set just because if they misbehave we will socially slash them? Why have PoS at all then and not just go to PoA or PoG?

tweets.text: RT @SpeechUnion: “As a writer and broadcaster in 2020s Britain, one almost expects the police eventually to arrive and allege some sort of thought crime, particularly if one writes about anti-Jewish racism and violence, free speech, the Middle East, Islam or trans issues. I write about all of them.” The Green Party is no friend of free speech. We saw that in its treatment of Dr Shahrar Ali, who was removed as the party’s Justice spokesperson and later expelled over his lawful gender-critical beliefs. Writing in The Spectator, Jonathan Sacerdoti recounts how the Green Party tried to have him arrested. One day, a plain-clothes police officer arrived at Jonathan’s door. As he points out, this was a rarity, given that nobody turned up when his car was broken into or when shoplifters threatened a local shop worker with a stolen bottle of wine. The officer suggested she come inside for a conversation. She informed Jonathan that she was there to invite him to a voluntary interview so he could give his “account”. The complaint related to a Green Party canvasser. Jonathan, the son of a Holocaust survivor, writes that he has become increasingly alarmed by the trajectory of the Green Party and the antisemitism emerging within it. Because he dared to challenge a representative of the party who appeared on his doorstep wearing a keffiyeh, he found himself facing a police visit. Jonathan had previously told another Green Party canvasser that he did not want the party canvassing at his home. It seems the Greens do not take kindly to voters who answer back and challenge them. The police officer also revealed something deeply concerning. It was not the woman in the keffiyeh who had made the harassment complaint. It was the earlier canvasser, who, the officer revealed, was then a Green Party candidate and is now a councillor. She alleged that Jonathan had called her “terrorist scum”, even though he had not. More troubling still, according to the officer, the Green Party appeared to have a “system” for collating intelligence about Jonathan. Jonathan writes, in response to the allegation of harassment: “Harassment in law requires a course of conduct involving at least two separate incidents, aimed at the same person. I didn’t know either woman, didn’t know where they lived or worked, or in fact anything about them other than their allegiance to the nasty party. They knew where I live, what I do, my ethnicity and religion, and even my husband’s name. I know who I think was harassing who.” After the officer left, Jonathan contacted his lawyer, who is funded by the Free Speech Union. He writes: “The complainant, whom they insisted on calling the ‘victim’, was pressing them to act, though the CPS itself recognised the weakness of an allegation with literally no evidence. Maybe, they said, I’d like to write a letter of regret, to make this all disappear? “Regret? For what? I’d broken no law. I declined. If ‘voluntary interviews’ and letters of regret are becoming the new tools for silencing lawful political speech, we must refuse them at every opportunity. “The irony is that the Green Party has shown far less sensitivity toward prejudice in its own ranks.” It is incredible that the police even investigated this. The Free Speech Union was pleased to have been able to help. Read more below 👇
